text:
I turn my eyes toward my own history.

Dreams, more dreams and more dreams… glory,

more glory… hatred… a nightingale fleeing…

and I am astonished not to see in all of it

a feature, a sketch, or a trace

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.


I turn again to look along the road traveled…

My march was a soldier's march,

with a victorious step, amid all the din;

my joy a barbarous joy…

And nowhere yet is there the shadow

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.


A summit rose before me; a thousand others tried

to crown it and could not;

only I remained above, smiling,

and there, with my voice released, my arm outstretched,

I never felt even the slightest peck

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.


I turned my brow toward the most beautiful sunset…

a thousand brave men yielded to defeat,

but I was victor over the terrible evil;

I was purple, evening glory,

without sensing the clandestine march

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.


Forces and powers besieged me

and, trial upon trial, hemmed in

my faith, which I neither exchange nor sell,

and I watched them march away in spite

of their spite, happy, without sensing anything in my breast

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.


Women… for my glory and my struggles

many were given to me in many places,

and everywhere I fell asleep loving,

and in the morning I went on toward another love,

but in none did I sense the dart

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.


And one day came the awkward circumstance

of our being alone in the room,

reading together without reading,

looking into each other's eyes without malice,

and afterward remaining with the delight

of the sweet sickness with which I am dying.

translation.title: The Sweet Sickness
translation.editorial_note: The translation preserves the repeated refrain and the movement from public glory to private recognition of the “sweet sickness.”
